analysis.one_liner: Caps bank overdraft fees and bans fees on declined debit card transactions.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap overdraft fees at one per month and ban most debit-card overdraft charges died in the House Financial Services Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have limited how banks charge overdraft fees. Banks could charge at most one overdraft fee a month and six a year per account, could not charge any nonsufficient-fund fee on ATM or debit card transactions, and would have to warn customers before a transaction triggers a fee. It would also stop banks from reordering transactions to trigger more fees and make them disclose the overdraft fee as an annual percentage rate, so customers could see how expensive it really is. It never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who overdraw their checking accounts, most often low- and moderate-income households, would pay far less in fees: banks could charge no more than one overdraft fee a month and six a year per account, no nonsufficient-fund fee on any ATM or debit card transaction, and no fee caused by a debit hold larger than the actual purchase. Customers would also get clearer disclosures, an annual-percentage-rate comparison, warnings at the ATM before a fee is charged, and protection from banks reordering transactions to maximize fees.

how_it_helps.text: Caps overdraft coverage fees at one per calendar month and six per calendar year per account, ending the practice of stacking multiple fees on a single day.
Bans nonsufficient-fund fees on ATM and debit card transactions entirely, so a declined card costs the customer nothing.
Requires banks to disclose the overdraft fee expressed as an annual percentage rate, exposing that a flat fee on a small purchase can equal an extremely high-cost loan.

Requires banks to post transactions in an order that does not create avoidable overdraft fees, to warn customers at ATMs before fees are triggered, and to bar charging fees when the overdraft results only from a debit hold larger than the actual purchase.
Bars banks from counting overdraft coverage as part of the account balance, so customers see their real money instead of money they would be charged to use.

analysis.who_pays: Banks and other depository institutions would lose a large fee revenue stream from overdraft and nonsufficient-fund charges, and might offset it with other account fees or scaled-back free services.

drawbacks.text: The bill caps overdraft fees but does not cap the amount itself beyond requiring fees to be 'reasonable and proportional' to the overdraft, leaving the CFPB to define that through future rulemaking, which could make the protection slower and weaker in practice.

By limiting banks to six overdraft fees per account per year, the bill could lead banks to offset lost revenue through other account fees or to scale back overdraft coverage programs, shifting costs onto customers in different forms.
The effective date is one year after enactment, with up to 24 months for CFPB rules, so relief for consumers would be delayed well beyond passage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are substantial: capping fees at six per year, requiring real-time warnings at ATMs, banning misleading balance displays and reordering of transactions, and disclosing fees as an annual percentage rate would directly cut a multibillion-dollar fee stream that falls hardest on low- and moderate-income customers. The strongest good-faith objections are that fee caps could lead banks to raise other account fees or limit services, and that banks argue overdraft coverage is a service that lets small purchases go through rather than be declined. But because the bill targets abusive marketing and fee frequency rather than banning coverage, and because the fees it limits are widely characterized as effectively high-cost short-term credit, the consumer benefit clearly outweighs the acknowledged costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee and then a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn Maloney introduced the Overdraft Protection Act of 2012 on May 9, 2012, with 46 original cosponsors joining her.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the day it was introduced.
On June 1, 2012, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit.
No further action was taken; the bill sat in committee and expired when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and other depository institutions that collect overdraft and nonsufficient-fund fees are better off, because the fee limits and bans were never enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks collecting overdraft and NSF fees

for.name: Rep. Carolyn Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its sponsor.

against.name: Banking industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation restricting overdraft fees, which are a major revenue source, as they had successfully done against earlier versions of similar bills.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill: no hearing, no markup, and no vote was ever scheduled, so the bill never left committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 50 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill sat in a House committee controlled by a Republican majority that took no action on it.

industries.industry: Retail banks and other depository institutions
industries.note: Banks would lose a major fee revenue stream: fee frequency caps, bans on most NSF fees on debit transactions, posting-order and debit-hold rules, and APR disclosure all directly cut into overdraft income. The bill's own findings describe these fees as falling hardest on low- and moderate-income consumers.

The bill bars banks from reporting negative overdraft information to credit bureaus when the overdraft is repaid, limiting how much overdraft data flows into the credit reporting system; bureaus gain little from this bill.
The bill makes the CFPB the rulemaking and enforcement authority for overdraft practices and directs a study of prepaid card overdraft, expanding its consumer-finance jurisdiction.
